summary.text: For \(n=9\), direct multiplication gives \((2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19\cdot23)^2+1=29^2\cdot59180057841661\), so this term is not squarefree. Thus the combined claim is false, independently of whether infinitely many other terms are prime.

full_proof.text:
Let \(p_0=2,p_1=3,p_2=5,\ldots\) denote the primes in increasing order, and define
\[
P_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}p_k,
\qquad
a(n)=P_n^2+1.
\]
(For \(n=0\), the empty product is \(1\), so \(a(0)=2\), in agreement with the stated indexing.) We will disprove the assertion that every \(a(n)\) is squarefree by exhibiting a square divisor of \(a(9)\).

The first nine primes are
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23.
\]
Indeed, these are prime, and every positive integer strictly between consecutive entries in this list, beginning after \(2\), is composite. Their cumulative products are
\[
\begin{aligned}
2&=2,\\
2\cdot3&=6,\\
2\cdot3\cdot5&=30,\\
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7&=210,\\
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11&=2310,\\
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13&=30030,\\
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17&=510510,\\
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19&=9699690,\\
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19\cdot23&=223092870.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
P_9=223092870
\]
and hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(9)
  &=223092870^2+1\\
  &=49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901.
\end{aligned}
\]
This integer has the exact factorization
\[
49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901
 =841\cdot59{,}180{,}057{,}841{,}661.
\]
The displayed multiplication can be checked directly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
59{,}180{,}057{,}841{,}661\cdot841
&=59{,}180{,}057{,}841{,}661\cdot(800+40+1)\\
&=47{,}344{,}046{,}273{,}328{,}800\\
&\quad+2{,}367{,}202{,}313{,}666{,}440\\
&\quad+59{,}180{,}057{,}841{,}661\\
&=49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(841=29^2\), it follows that
\[
29^2\mid a(9).
\]
Moreover, \(29>1\).

Recall that a positive integer is squarefree precisely when it is not divisible by the square of any integer greater than \(1\). Equivalently, if \(N\) is squarefree and \(d^2\mid N\), then \(d\) must be a unit; among the natural numbers the only unit is \(1\). Applying this with \(N=a(9)\) and \(d=29\) would force \(29=1\), which is impossible. Therefore
\[
a(9)\text{ is not squarefree}.
\]

Thus the universal claim
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N,\quad a(n)\text{ is squarefree}
\]
is false. The conjecture in question asserts the conjunction of this universal squarefreeness claim with the claim that \(a(n)\) is prime for infinitely many \(n\). A conjunction is false as soon as either one of its components is false. Hence the explicit counterexample \(n=9\) disproves the combined conjecture, independently of whether infinitely many terms of the sequence are prime.
